Rick Steves' Highlights

Top Sights in Haarlem

From the bustling market square to a wartime hiding place and a time-warped 18th-century museum, Haarlem packs remarkable variety into its compact, walkable center.

Landmark Tap to expand
Grote Markt
Market Square — Heart of Haarlem

Where 10 streets converge, this has been Haarlem's delightful centerpiece for 700 years. A pedestrian zone now, it fills with market stalls on Saturdays and café tables every other day. Don't miss the L.J. Coster statue (the man who may have invented movable type before Gutenberg!), the 1630 Town Hall façade, and the Vleeshal (Meat Market) with its Flemish Renaissance carvings.

👾 Tip: Look for the sheep and cow carvings on the outside of the Vleeshal — they were carved to show what was sold inside the building. The butchers' and leatherworkers' guilds built it in 1603.
Historic Church Tap to expand
St. Bavo's Church
Grote Kerk — The Great Church

Haarlem's Gothic masterpiece, visible for miles across the flat Dutch landscape. Built over 150 years (c. 1390–1540), it houses Holland's greatest pipe organ, the grave of painter Frans Hals, intricate medieval carvings, model ships, and 16 remarkable features to discover on a self-guided tour. Allow at least 45 minutes — see our full St. Bavo's section below.

🎵 Tip: Mozart was just 10 years old when he played this organ in 1766, near the end of a three-year tour of Europe. Handel played here in 1740. With 5,068 pipes ranging from a few inches to over 20 feet tall, the sound fills the entire church.
Historic Museum Tap to expand
Teylers Museum
Oldest Museum in the Netherlands

Opened in 1784, the Teylers is a "museum of a museum" — a perfectly preserved 18th-century collection of fossils, minerals, primitive electronic gadgets, and early technology. The centerpiece Oval Room is a temple of science and learning. The newly restored home of founder Pieter Teyler is attached, including a miniature model of the house exactly as it appeared on the day he died. Two lovely painting galleries are hung floor-to-ceiling in old-style salon fashion.

🔬 Tip: Look for the "highest point in Europe" on display — the very top of Mont Blanc, Europe's highest peak, brought to one of Europe's lowest countries. The Teylers collection is full of surprises like this.
WWII Museum Tap to expand
Corrie ten Boom House
The Hiding Place — A WWII Story

This clock shop was the center of one of WWII's most courageous operations. The Ten Boom family hid Jews from the Nazis in a secret room barely a yard deep — "the hiding place." When the Gestapo raided on February 28, 1944, four Jews and two resistance fighters stayed hidden for 47 hours undetected. In all, the family saved about 800 people. Access is by tour only (reservations essential), and available only in your language.

🕵️ Tip: The hiding place was less than a yard deep — yet six people hid inside for 47 hours undetected when the Gestapo raided. The tour is available only in your own language, so reservations are essential.
Historic Landmark Tap to expand
Windmill De Adriaan
Clamber Around a Working Mill

Haarlem has a windmill that visitors can actually explore inside — a rare hands-on treat. Windmills were the engines of the Dutch Golden Age, draining the flooded polderland and powering sawmills and grain mills. Climbing inside gives you a real sense of Dutch engineering ingenuity and the scale of these remarkable machines.

⚙️ Tip: Windmills were the engines of the Dutch Golden Age — draining flooded polderland and powering grain mills and sawmills. Climbing inside De Adriaan gives you a real sense of how these machines worked and why they mattered so much to Dutch life.
Art & Culture Tap to expand
Frans Hals Museum
Haarlem's Famous Son

Haarlem's top art museum showcases the work of portrait master Frans Hals — one of the greatest painters of the Dutch Golden Age. Hals moved to Haarlem as a child and lived here his entire life, painting mayors, preachers, and tavern revelers with remarkable energy. He had 10 children and produced hundreds of masterpieces. (He's actually buried under the floor of St. Bavo's Church — look for his grave!) The museum also has a secondary "Hal" location in the old Meat Market on the Grote Markt.

🖌️ Tip: Frans Hals was famous for capturing expressions so alive and spontaneous they look almost like photos. Look for the smiling, laughing figures — they're unlike any paintings of the time. Totally ahead of his era.

Self-Guided Tour

St. Bavo's Church — 16 Things to Find

Enter from the Grote Markt side near the north transept. Walk to the center where the nave meets the transept and begin your exploration. Rick Steves recommends allowing 45 minutes — here's what to look for.

1
Center of Church Viewpoint
Simple white walls, a black floor, a brown ceiling, and a mahogany organ create a vast, airy space. Built over 150 years, the architecture is surprisingly uniform. Look up: fan-vaulted cedar ceiling (1530). Look down: tombstones paving the floor. Spot "squatting characters" supporting the pilasters halfway up the walls.
2
The Choir & Misericords
The oldest part of the church. While commoners stood during services, nobles perched on tiny ledges called misericords (carved in 1512). Find the stall showing a poor peasant bending over to support a rich man's backside. The stalls are decorated with coats of arms of noble families.
3
Grave of Frans Hals
A simple floor slab marked with a lantern — just right of center in the choir floor, labeled "Graf van Frans Hals." Haarlem's beloved portrait master of the Golden Age is buried right here, in the church where he worshipped his whole life.
4
The Pillar Biters
Knee-level carvings at both ends of the brass barrier. The man wears pointy Dutch overshoes; the woman wears a fashionable turban and rosary beads. The message: don't go overboard on religious devotion. A medieval warning against being "more Catholic than the pope."
5
Three Little Ships
Suspended between columns, these model ships sail under the Dutch flag and the rearing lion flag. The largest is a frigate — the fast, three-masted warships that protected Dutch merchant vessels on their two-year journeys to the Far East. Notice the flat-bottomed hull (needed for Amsterdam's shallow harbor) and the iron saw on the keel for slicing harbor chains.
6
Hydraulic Engineers Memorial
A marble relief showing Neptune in his water chariot, honoring Christiaan Brunings and Frederik Willem Conrad. In flood-prone Holland, hydraulic engineers were genuine heroes — their work determined whether people lived or died.
7
Brewers' Chapel (Brouwerskapel)
This chapel marks Haarlem's 750-year history in a delightful way — featuring the extremes of human size. Look for the height markers of the city's smallest and tallest citizens on the central pillar.
8
Height Marks: Simon Paap & Daniel Cajanus
Black marks on the chapel pillar record the heights of Haarlem's shortest citizen (Simon Paap, 33 inches — who reportedly died in a dwarf-tossing incident!) and tallest (Daniel Cajanus, 8 feet 8 inches). A genuinely jaw-dropping comparison.
9
Old Map of "Harlemum" (1688)
Shows the walled city with ramparts, moat, and surrounding panels illustrating 750 years of history. The lower-left panel shows the dramatic 1572–73 Siege of Haarlem, with women fighting alongside men against Spanish troops.
10
Ornate Calligraphy Roster (1736)
The fifth roster on the right, from 1736, features mesmerizingly elaborate calligraphy listing prominent church members. An example of the incredible penmanship skill of the era.
11
Pelican Lectern
A brass lectern from 1499. According to medieval legend, pelicans feed their young with their own blood — making the pelican a symbol of Christ's self-sacrifice. This one looks exactly like a pelican stabbing itself... except it actually looks like an eagle. Apparently, its creator had never seen a real pelican.
12
Peace & Tolerance Window
A vibrant stained-glass window designed by Michel van Overbeeke, dedicated in 2008. A cloak of red roses amid a cosmic blue swirl promotes religious harmony while hinting at Christian themes. Nearby, small relief statues with beheaded bodies and defaced faces commemorate victims of the 1566 Iconoclastic Fury.
13
Dog-Whipper's Chapel
A sculpted relief (top of a column) shows an angry man whipping an angry dog while striding over another dog's head. Back when churches served as rainy-day marketplaces, this man's actual job was to keep Haarlem's dogs out of the church. His title? Dog-Whipper. Officially.
14
Model of the Church
A glass box holding a scale model 100 times smaller than the church itself. This miniature masterpiece took over 1,000 work-hours to build. Look closely for the matchsticks, washers, screens, glue, wire, and paper clips used to construct it — remarkable detail work.
15
Church Strongbox
A heavy wood-and-iron chest that served as the church's safe for cash and precious documents — including papers granting the power to sell indulgences (forgiveness for sins). This was big business in medieval Catholicism, and one of the abuses that sparked the Protestant Reformation.
16
Cannonball in the Wall
Placed here in 1573, this cannonball commemorates Haarlem's finest hour: the heroic seven-month Siege of Haarlem. In the winter of 1572–73, Haarlem proclaimed independence from Spain. The Spanish governor besieged the city. Cold, hungry, with even women joining men on the barricades — Haarlem held out for seven months before surrendering. Their brave stand became the Dutch Alamo, inspiring the entire country to keep fighting.
⛪

The Choir

Built first, the choir was used for worship for over a century while the rest of the church was completed. The brass-and-wood barrier keeps visitors from the most sacred area, just as peasants were kept out in medieval times. The misericord ledges (carved 1512) let wealthy patrons rest their backs in the wooden choir stalls during long services. The phrase "stinking rich" reportedly originated here — wealthy people paid to be buried under the church floor, but embalmed or not, they smelled.

🗣️

The Pulpit

Elaborately carved from oak in 1679, the pulpit is topped with a tower-shaped roof. Brass handrails snake down the staircase — actually carved as serpents fleeing the word of God. In this simply decorated Protestant church, the pulpit is the most ornate element, directing the congregation's eyes to the preacher. After the Protestant Reformation, teaching became more important than ritual, giving the pulpit a higher profile than the altar.

🎵

The Great Organ

Finished in 1738 by Amsterdam's Christian Müller, this organ stands 100 feet high with 5,068 pipes, three keyboards, a forest of pedals, and 65 stops. Its mahogany-colored casing is studded with statues of musicians and an eight-piece combo of angels. Lions on top hold Haarlem's coat of arms with the motto "Virtue Conquers Violence." A 20-foot pipe rumbles the rafters; the smallest pipe is just a few inches long. Both Handel (1740) and a 10-year-old Mozart (1766) played it. Albert Schweitzer also performed here.

From the 10th century to today

Haarlem Through the Ages

Over a thousand years of history shaped this remarkable city — from a sandy forest clearing to a Golden Age powerhouse, and through war and occupation to the vibrant town you visit today.

10th Century
🌲 Harulahaima — "House in the Forest"
Haarlem's earliest records describe wooden farmhouses, noble towers, a church, monasteries, and a comital court on open sandy ground in the forest. The name comes from the Frankish word Harulahaima. Archaeological evidence including 11th-century skeletal remains confirms continuous habitation from this era.
12th Century
🏰 Counts of Holland Take Notice
Haarlem's strategic position along the coastal barrier prompts the Counts of Holland to establish a fortified outpost, transforming the settlement into a key administrative center. The Haarlemse Beek stream feeds early brewing and textile industries, while the Spaarne River junction enables toll collection from traders. Haarlem becomes a walled town.
1245
📜 City Charter Granted
On November 23, Count William II formally grants Haarlem its city charter (stadsrechten), giving citizens the right to independent judicial administration. The new legal status attracts merchants and artisans, sparking rapid growth. Stone buildings begin replacing timber, and luxury pottery production — possibly unique in all of Holland — emerges. Dominican and Carmelite monasteries expand.
14th–15th Century
⚓ A City on the Rise
Haarlem grows into one of Holland's most influential cities, second only to Dordrecht, driven by textiles, beer, and shipbuilding. By 1422, a four-kilometer moat, gates, and walls enclose a city of roughly 8,000 inhabitants. Weavers arrive from Flanders, Brabant, and Wallonia, and more than 20 monasteries occupy over 10% of urban space.
1566–1578
✝️ Reformation and Religious Upheaval
Protestant ideas spread through the city, though Haarlem's civic leaders carefully guard the Grote Kerk to prevent the mob violence that destroys hundreds of churches across the Low Countries in 1566. In 1578, the city council officially adopts the Protestant Reformation, converting the Grote Kerk to Reformed use. Catholic imagery is removed by municipal decree, the interior is whitewashed, and the focus shifts from ritual to preaching.
1572–1573
⚔️ The Siege of Haarlem — The Dutch Alamo
Haarlem aligns with William of Orange's revolt against Habsburg Spain. Spanish forces under the Duke of Alba besiege the city with 16,000–20,000 troops. For seven brutal months, 4,000 defenders hold out through a freezing winter, with women joining men on the barricades. By July 1573, starvation forces surrender. Spanish commanders execute 2,000–2,300 defenders. Yet Haarlem's resistance galvanizes the Dutch independence movement — inspiring Alkmaar, Leiden, and ultimately the entire Dutch Republic.
1600–1700
🌷 The Golden Age
Protestant refugees from Spanish-controlled Antwerp flood into Haarlem, supercharging the linen textile trade. Population surges from 18,000 to over 35,000 by 1630. Tulip cultivation, introduced from Ottoman bulbs in the 1590s, turns Haarlem's sandy outskirts into the horticultural capital of Europe — fueling the famous 1636–37 tulip mania. Frans Hals revolutionizes portraiture at his Haarlem studio, while printmakers and painters make the city an artistic hub rivaling Amsterdam.
1752–1784
🔬 An Age of Enlightenment
Even as the Dutch economy stagnates, Haarlem becomes an intellectual hub. The Hollandsche Maatschappij der Wetenschappen — the Netherlands' oldest learned society — is founded in 1752. In 1778, silk merchant Pieter Teyler van der Hulst bequeaths his fortune to establish what becomes the Netherlands' first public museum, opening in 1784 with fossils, minerals, scientific instruments, and art collections guided by Enlightenment ideals.
1839
🚂 The First Railway in the Netherlands
On September 20, the Netherlands' very first steam railway line opens — connecting Haarlem to Amsterdam. This 20-kilometer route transforms Haarlem's economic fortunes, enabling efficient commuting and goods transport. The line extends to Leiden in 1843, integrating Haarlem into a national network and laying the groundwork for 19th-century industrial growth in printing, shipbuilding, and cocoa processing.
1940–1945
🕍 Nazi Occupation and Resistance
German forces enter Haarlem on May 15, 1940. The ten Boom family converts their watch shop into a hiding place for Jews and resistance workers, sheltering an estimated 800 people before their arrest in February 1944. Student resistance fighter Hannie Schaft operates in the city, assassinating Dutch collaborators until her capture and execution in the dunes in March 1945. The brutal Hunger Winter of 1944–45 drives residents to eat tulip bulbs for survival. Canadian forces liberate Haarlem on May 8, 1945.
Post-1945
🏗️ Rebuilding and Modern Haarlem
Haarlem rebuilds rapidly under national reconstruction programs. Population grows from 150,000 in 1947 to 170,000 by 1960, spurring new residential districts designed as self-contained communities with schools, parks, and shops. The Waarderpolder industrial estate opens in the 1960s, relocating businesses from the historic center. Today, Haarlem is a thriving, beautifully preserved city where centuries of history are still visible on every corner.

Famous Haarlemmers

Notable People of Haarlem

From a painter who defined the Dutch Golden Age to a woman who defied the Nazis, Haarlem has produced some remarkable people whose stories still resonate today.

🖌️
Frans Hals
c. 1582 – 1666
Haarlem's most celebrated artist moved to the city as a child and spent his entire life here. A friend of mayors and preachers, he painted hundreds of masterpieces capturing middle-class citizens and tavern life with extraordinary vitality. He had 10 children and died at about 84 — old for the era. His grave is in St. Bavo's Church, and his work fills the Frans Hals Museum.
🕰️
Corrie ten Boom
1892 – 1983
A devout Christian clockmaker who, with her family, hid Jews and resistance fighters from the Nazis in a secret room above the family clock shop. When the Gestapo raided in 1944, the hidden fugitives went undetected. Corrie survived the Ravensbrück concentration camp and told her story in the 1971 memoir The Hiding Place, which became a global inspiration.
🔬
Pieter Teyler van der Hulst
1702 – 1778
A silk merchant and philanthropist who willed the equivalent of €80 million (in today's value) to found a museum dedicated to "stimulating art and science." The Teylers Museum opened in 1784, six years after his death, and his last bequest wasn't spent until 1983 — over two centuries of cultural generosity. His restored home is now part of the museum.
🖨️
Laurens Janszoon Coster
c. 1370 – 1440
Haarlem's claim to one of history's greatest inventions. Coster reportedly carved a letter from wood and saw its imprint in wet sand — giving him the idea of movable type. Haarlemmers credit him with inventing modern printing before Gutenberg. His statue on the Grote Markt shows him proudly holding up a block of type. The historical debate continues.

Content based on Rick Steves' Netherlands travel guide and St. Bavo's Church historical sources.
